Hi Michel,

I went through your GWAS by subtraction tutorial (https://rpubs.com/MichelNivard/565885). Thanks for writing it. 
I am finding it difficult to understand what's happening in the modeling equations 

In the model without SNPs, you write, 

model<-'C=~NA*EA + start(0.4)*CP
        NC=~NA*EA
         
         NC~~1*NC
         C~~1*C
         C~~0*NC

         CP ~~ 0*EA
         CP~~0*CP
         EA~~0*EA'

I have highlighted the parts that I don't understand. What's NA here? What's start(0.4) ?

In the model with SNPs, you write, 

model<-'C=~NA*EA +start(0.2)*EA + start(0.5)*CP
         NC=~NA*EA +start(0.2)*EA
         
         C~SNP
         NC~SNP

         NC~~1*NC
         C~~1*C
         C~~0*NC

         CP ~~ 0*EA
         CP~~0*CP
         EA~~0*EA
         SNP~~SNP'

Why is the equation of the model with SNPs is so different from the equation of the model without SNP (apart from the SNP parts: C~SNP and NC~SNP)? 
If I have to run a GWAS by subtraction between two phenotypes, e.g. schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, will the equation will be the same as here?
How to know what number to use inside start(xx) in the equation? I am sorry for being naive here. I am not familiar with structural equations. I'd be thankful if you can explain these equations in a more detailed manner. 

Also, previously (before this tutorial was posted) I asked a similar question in Github and Elliot replied with a link to a tutorial. (https://github.com/MichelNivard/GenomicSEM/issues/12). Based on that, I wrote the equation as follows. 

model1 <- 'BPD  ~ SNP

After seeing your new tutorial, Now I am worried that I've been doing it wrong. Could you please clarify these, please. 

Thanks again for your help. 

Regards
Veera

parts:
Dear Veera,

These are all good questions.

First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.

Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). Or for example, a value above zero and less than 1.0 for the genetic variance of a GWAS phenotype (because we know that its SNP heritability is greater than 0 and far less than 1.0) Overriding the defaults if often unnecessary, but can be helpful for the reasons I outline here.

I think that some of these clarifications are worth putting into our tutorial. We'll put it on our to do list. In the meantime, feel free to reach out with further questions.

All the best,

Elliot

P.S. If you are looking for a very brief introduction to SEM, I suggest McArdle & Boker's Path Analysis and Path Diagrams chapter (https://doi.org/10.1002/0470013192.bsa471). Accessible books are Loehlin's Latent Variable Models and Kline's Principals and Practices of Structural Equation Modeling, both of which I use in my graduate SEM course. A much more advanced book is Bollen's Structural Equations with Latent Variables.

Dear Elliot,

Thanks a lot. You are so kind to take the time to write a detailed response to my question. I really appreciate the effort. 
I wanted to understand this properly as I have plans to use this approach for more than one project. So, I went ahead and ran the GWIS analysis for EA3 and Cognitive performance (CP) using the summary statistics available from SSGAC. I believe that these same summary files were used for generating the Cog and Noncog summary stats that your team has made available for public use. I generated Cog (CP minus EA3) and Nocog (EA3 minus cog) summary files using the formula from your slides. I'll call these as Cog.residual and Noncog.residual. Then I compared these summary files with your Cog and Noncog summary files, which I'll call Cog.cholesky and Noncog.cholesky. 

I did genetic correlations between these four summary files. The results are shown in this table. I see a full correlation between Noncog.cholesky and Noncog.residual. But the genetic correlation between Cog.cholesky and Cog.residual is not 1, but 0.72. I can understand why this is so. Based on the Cholesky method equation, Cog is not really just CP, but its CP + EA. However, based on the residual method, CP is just CP without EA. I am assuming that's why the genetic correlation is not perfectly one. Is that right? Then, I see that using the Cholesky method, the rg between Cog and Noncog is zero. I assume that this is by design, as you include "C~~0*NC" in the SEM equation. However, using the residual method, the genetic correlation between Cog and Noncog is strongly negative (rg=0.68; SE=0.01; P=0). Even the genetic correlation between cog.residual and Noncog.cholesky is is also -0.68. I am wondering if this is an artifact relationship arising due to the way the genomic SEM works or if this is an interpretable relationship? 

Then, I also estimated the heritability using LDSC methods. The results are shown in the table below. There is only a moderate difference between Noncog.cholesky and Noncog.residual. However, there is a large difference between Cog.cholesky and Cog.residual, like the h2 of Cog.cholesky is two times the h2 of Cog.residual. I am assuming this is also due to that Cog.cholesky is not really just CP, but its CP +EA.  Correct me if I am wrong. 

Then I also visualized the scatter plot of BETA values between the Cholesky and residual methods. As you said, I see that the BETAs are slightly on different scales. The BETA correlations corroborate with rg values. I see a high correlation between BETAs of Noncog.cholesky and Noncog.residual. But a relatively lower correlation between the BETAs of Cog.cholesky and Cog.residual. 



xxx


Things are getting clearer. But I still didn't understand a few things. I'll list them. 
1. Which one is better? Cholesky or residual method?
2. Why did you choose the Cholesky method for the paper? And why did you choose to model the Cog as CP+EA, rather than just CP?
3. Is the negative rg between cog and noncog using the residual method, expected? Is there any biological explanation for that? If I used the residual method and write a paper, how should report this negative correlation in the paper?
4. How do you determine the sample size of the SEM derived phenotype? For now, I am using the same N as the original phenotypes. 
5. Is the heritability estimate of the SEM derived sumstats interpretable? Is there a reason why the h2 values of Cholesky method are larger than h2 values of the residual method. 

I hope I'm not disturbing you a lot. I believe your answers will be useful not just for me, but also for many others who might see this post in the future.
Thanks again for your help.

Best regards
Veera

First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Dear Veera,

These are all good questions.

First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.

Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). OK, so I think I see at least part of where we are missing each other. You are estimating an EA-minus-Cog factor (i.e. a "NonCog" factor) in one model and a Cog-minus-EA factor (i.e a "non-EA" factor) in another model. Each of your two models outputs two sets of sumstats but you are discarding one set from each. This isn't what we are doing. In Demange et al., we fit a model that decomposes EA genetics into Cog genetics and NonCog genetics. We don't fit a model that decomposes Cog genetics into EA genetics and Non-EA genetics. You must be correlating your "Non-EA" factor (what you call Cog-residual) with our Cognitive factor (which is just the original cognitive performance GWAS). If you want to validate that the regression based (slide 37) parameterization against the output from the Demange et al. Cholesky parameterization, you will only need to run the first of your two models to produce the Cog and NonCog sumstats. The Cog sumstats that you discard are indeed equivalent, apart from rescaling, to the Cog sumstats from Demange et al. The EA-minus-Cog sumstats that you retain are equivalent, apart from rescaling, to the NonCog sumstats from Demange et al. If you want to run the other model to residualize Cog from EA, you certainly can, but we have not done that so there is nothing from Demange et al. to compare your results to.

On Sunday, July 26, 2020 at 6:13:25 PM UTC+2 Elliot Tucker-Drob wrote:
Dear Veera,

These are all good questions.

First, absent coding typos (such as the missing + that you previously caught), the model from slide 37 from the talk I previously linked to and the model in the GWAS-by-Subtraction tutorial are equivalent. The "slide 37 model" implements GWAS-by-subtraction via regression whereas the "tutorial model" implements it via Cholesky decomposition. You can read more about Cholesky models in SEM contexts in this paper by Loehlin: https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02361160. The difference between the two implementations is that the "slide 37 model" keeps the two components (e.g. the "Cog" and "NonCog" components) in their original units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is its SNP heritability, whereas the "tutorial model" places the two components in Z-units, such that the total genetic variance of each component is equal to 1.0 (the units are not thrown out, as the information is now captured in the loadings on the Cholesky factors). The genetic correlations between sumstats formed from the two approaches will equal 1.0, and both approaches will produce equivalent genetic correlations (i.e. standardized covariances) with collateral phenotypes. Additionally, if you were to plot the SNP betas (e.g. for a subset of SNPs for ease) from the two approaches, you would also find that they are on different units but are perfectly correlated.

Second, you are correct regarding the use of NA and start(). NA freely estimates a parameter (lavaan's default is to fix the first loading to 1.0). start() provides a starting value other than the lavaan default (I believe that this often is a 1 or a 0 depending on the parameter). Numerical optimization is iterative, which means that the model is fit first using the starting values, then adjusts the values in increments or decrements and determines whether the adjustment has increased or reduced model fit, and does this over and over again until some convergence criterion is achieved indicating the the maximum fit has been achieved. There are various reasons for providing your own starting values. Some are: a) speeding up run-time (so fewer iterations are needed for a model to converge), b) facilitating model convergence (e.g., when the model "times out" and fails to converge using the default start values), c) preventing the model from converging on local fit maxima that depart from the global maximum, d) preventing the model from converging on an equivalent, but less interpretable, solution to the preferred solution (e.g. in some models with latent variables, such as the Cholesky, when all regression paths are negative, the solution is equivalent to the preferred solution with them all being positive; the negative solution provides the same interpretation, but the factors must be conceptualized as being "reverse coded," e.g. higher scores corresponding with lower education, which can be confusing). Useful start values are informed guesses about the likely parameter value, such as the estimate from a previous run of a simpler model (e.g. the model without the SNP). Or for example, a value above zero and less than 1.0 for the genetic variance of a GWAS phenotype (because we know that its SNP heritability is greater than 0 and far less than 1.0) Overriding the defaults if often unnecessary, but can be helpful for the reasons I outline here.

I think that some of these clarifications are worth putting into our tutorial. We'll put it on our to do list. In the meantime, feel free to reach out with further questions.

All the best,

Elliot

P.S. If you are looking for a very brief introduction to SEM, I suggest McArdle & Boker's Path Analysis and Path Diagrams chapter (https://doi.org/10.1002/0470013192.bsa471). Accessible books are Loehlin's Latent Variable Models and Kline's Principals and Practices of Structural Equation Modeling, both of which I use in my graduate SEM course. A much more advanced book is Bollen's Structural Equations with Latent Variables.
